q: Insertion sort on an already sorted array of n elements takes…
why: Each new element is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put: n − 1 comparisons, no shifts.

q: Selection sort on an already sorted array takes…
why: It still scans the whole remaining part to find each minimum: about n²/2 comparisons regardless of order.

q: Which of these is NOT stable?
why: Selection sort's long-distance swap can move an element past an equal one, changing their order.

options: Sorting by a second key keeps the order from a previous sort among equal elements
why: E.g. sort by name, then stable-sort by age: people with the same age stay alphabetical.

q: What is `a` after ONE pass of the outer loop (i = 1) of insertion sort on [5, 2, 4, 6]?
why: i = 1 picks up 2, shifts 5 right and puts 2 at index 0. The rest is untouched.

q: An array of 10⁶ numbers is almost sorted: only a handful of elements are out of place. Which elementary sort fits best?
why: Insertion sort's cost is proportional to how far elements are out of place, so nearly sorted input is close to O(n).
